newsitem.title: INDIA: Thai C/A deficit/GDP ratio to decline - minister.
newsitem.headline: Thai C/A deficit/GDP ratio to decline - minister.

text.p: Thailand expects its current-account deficit as a share of gross domestic product (GDP) to decline to about seven percent at the end of 1997 from 8.1 percent at the end of 1996, Commerce Minister Narongchai Akrasanee said on Friday.

Narongchai told Reuters in an interview in the Indian capital that Thailand aimed to slow down imports, increase exports and cut government spending to bring down the current account deficit as a share of GDP.
He said the relatively high current account deficit last year had created speculation that the value of the Thai baht would have to fall with respect to the U.S. dollar.
Narongchai said the baht had depreciated in the past 15 to 16 months against the dollar by about four percent, far less than the mark or the yen had dropped against the dollar.
"People speculate that the Thai baht must fall more than four percent," he said.

But Thailand is not willing to abandon the basket of currencies it uses to fix the baht's value, Narongchai said. The baht is pegged to a basket of currencies which is thought to be heavily weighted by the U.S. dollar.
"Nobody is comfortable but we have no option. We have to stick to this system," Narongchai said.
Thailand's relatively underdeveloped foreign exchange market meant the baht was prone to speculation, he said.
"If we let go of the basket speculators can do damage," he said, adding that Thailand has some $39 billion in reserves it can use to defend the baht.
